item.title: Bo Nix's stats continue to get worse in Year 3
item.dc:creator: Michael David Smith
item.description: By just about any measure, Nix is playing his worst football this season.
item.content:encoded:
When you draft a quarterback in the first round, you hope to see him improve over his first few years in the league. That is most certainly not what has happened for the Broncos with Bo Nix.

After Nix's disastrous performance in the Broncos' Black Friday loss against the Steelers, it's fair to say that Nix is only getting worse. By just about any statistical measure you can look at, Nix is playing his worst football in Year 3.

Nix's passer rating is a career-low 79.0, down from 87.8 in 2025 and 93.3 in 2024.

Nix's yards-per-pass average is a career-low 5.9, down from 6.4 in 2025 and 6.7 in 2024.

Nix's completion rate is a career-low 59.4 percent, down from 63.4 percent in 2025 and 66.3 percent in 2024.

Nix has thrown touchdowns on a career-low 3.3 percent of his passes, down from 4.1 percent in 2025 and 5.1 percent in 2024.

Nix is averaging a career-low 193.1 passing yards per game, down from 231.2 in 2025 and 222.1 in 2024.

Running the ball, Nix has become completely ineffective, averaging just 2.9 yards per carry after averaging 4.3 in 2025 and 4.7 in 2024. Nix's rushing first downs have declined from 45 in 2024 to 25 in 2025 to just 12 this year.

Despite their quarterback taking a step backward, the Broncos are 8-3 and in first place in the AFC West. There's every reason to believe Denver will be in the playoffs.

But the Broncos aren't going to be able to do anything in the playoffs if Nix plays like he did against the Steelers. And the trends suggest Nix is only getting worse.

item.title: The Caleb Williams second contract looms, possibly sooner than anyone realizes
item.dc:creator: Mike Florio
item.description: Williams becomes eligible for a new deal after Week 18, not after the postseason.
item.content:encoded:
Football is business. It's big business, and it's getting bigger all the time.

For the league and the teams, it's perfectly acceptable (in the eyes of the media and the fans) for them to treat football as the big business it is. When players do it, many bristle. The players, they'll say, should be happy they're being paid to play a game.

They have enough, why would they want more?

It's a warped view of what the football business is. It's for the league and the teams to maximize the revenue. It's for the players to maximize their salaries.

And if it's OK, for instance, for the league and the teams to push for 18 regular-season games or to peel Sunday contests away for more standalone weekday windows or to hopscotch the globe in an effort to make the sport an international powerhouse, a player should be allowed to be aggressive about his own financial position, too. He's not being selfish; he's being smart.

Enter Bears quarterback Caleb Williams. Even before he was drafted, Caleb and his father, Carl, were exploring business ideas for maximizing Caleb's compensation. Carl, when speaking to agents, floated the idea of Caleb getting a slice of equity in the team that drafts him. (The NFL, at about the same time, changed the rules to seal off that possibility.) Caleb and Carl, as we've heard it, also considered creative concepts for minimizing the tax burden (like the owners always do), such as having Caleb's wages paid into an LLC.

While none of their creative and potentially innovative concepts worked, there's an obvious device hiding in plain sight. At Article 7, Section 3(k)(1) of the Collective Bargaining Agreement: "A Rookie Contract for a Drafted Rookie may not be renegotiated, amended or altered in any way until after the final regular season game of the player’s third contract year."

The common belief is that a drafted player can get a second contract after his third season. The key term is "regular season."

With Caleb Williams in his third season and the Bears at 9-2, there undoubtedly will be a postseason after his third regular season. Why shouldn't he — and why wouldn't he — want his second contract to be finalized in the window between the end of the 2026 regular season and the start of the 2026 postseason?

Beyond the fact that he has earned much more than he has been paid (thanks to a rookie wage scale aimed at keeping first-round busts from absconding with wealth they'll never earn), Williams continues to carry the injury risk. The second contract shifts the injury risk to the team. He should want that transfer of risk to happen as soon as possible.

The problem is leverage. Williams isn't going to refuse to play in the playoffs, even if he simply cites an "injury" to justify sitting out until he gets his contract. He's all about the team, and that concept becomes even more important in the aftermath of Aaron Rodgers's ultimate anti-team move from only three days ago.

Here's what Caleb can do. He can send a very simple and direct message, if he's willing to say it — and if he's willing to follow through on it. He can tell the Bears, "Extend my contract before the first playoff game to a market-level deal or I will not sign a second contract until I become an unrestricted free agent."

It won't be easy, because the system is rigged against the players. Williams would have to finish his four-year rookie deal, his fifth-year option, and at least two (if not three) franchise tags before forcing his way to the open market. That's up to eight seasons without getting the second contract he has earned.

That said, if any player can pull it off, it's a quarterback. The risk of a career-altering injury (while not zero) is smaller than it is for the other positions. After his eighth NFL season (2031), Williams will have recently turned 30 — which is young relative to the other positions.

For the Bears, it would be prudent to get it done sooner than later. If Williams keeps performing like he has (and if he keeps improving), it'll never get any cheaper than it will be after Week 18 of the 2026 regular season. The market will keep going up, and the salary cap will keep going up. Williams's value, in turn, will keep going up.

It's something to watch over the next six weeks. Even if the deal can't be done until after Chicago's Week 18 game at Minnesota concludes on January 9 or January 10, 2027, unofficial advance conversations can begin at any time.

All of this will surely make Bears fans nervous. But if the Bears are willing and able to become the first team to sign a draft pick in the window between the end of a player's third regular season and the start of the playoffs, Williams's future could be secured in Chicago for years to come.

And if Williams attempts to pursue this approach, no one should be upset. It's strictly business. The same kind of business the league and the owners would conduct, if they were in that same position.

item.title: It's time for the clock to have tenths of a second
item.dc:creator: Mike Florio
item.description: Football is a game of clear margins, but the time element remains a little too fuzzy.
item.content:encoded:
Football is a game of inches. And a game of seconds.

More accurately, it's a game of margins. Small margins. Victory (and defeat) often resides in those margins.

That makes the rules regarding those margins even more important. And that's why the operation of the clock in the final seconds of Thursday's Chiefs-Bills game seemed to be so significant. Especially since it appeared that Kansas City's final drive left four extra seconds for Buffalo to score the game-winning field goal. Which happened with the final snap showing four seconds on the clock.

The NFL pushed back on that perception on Friday, telling Mark Maske of Front Office Sports that there was no clock error. That the first-down shotgun snap muffed by quarterback Patrick Mahomes and recovered in a scrum by Mahomes with the whistle eventually blowing and Bills coach Joe Brady (as NBC's Mike Tirico described it) "running down to take a timeout" justifiably resulted in the clock moving only one second.

The clock, as Tirico said after the play, showed 19 seconds. It appeared that the whistle blew with 22 seconds left. The clock ended up restoring the time to 25 seconds, after a play that began with 26 seconds on the clock. Which defies common sense and the general notion that the passage of time is objective.

(Maske didn't address the second-down play, a five-yard run from tailback Emmett Johnson that had the whistle blow with 19 seconds left — before the clock magically jumped back to 20.)

Regardless of whether the vague and not-generally-known "officiating mechanics" somehow allow a snap, fumble, recovery, whistle, and a coach "running down to take a timeout" to justifiably consume only one second of clock time, precision matters in the moments approaching the expiration of the game. One way to achieve full precision would be to incorporate tenths of a second in the final minute of a quarter, like other time-based sports do.

As explained in the aftermath of the Michigan clock debacle that turned a Wolverines loss into a win on Labor Day weekend, the Eagles proposed adding tenths of a second twice in recent years, in 2023 and 2024. The effort failed because many of the existing clocks weren’t capable of showing tenths of seconds, and teams didn’t want to spend the money to adapt to the new rule.

It could return, we're told. The league has in recent months (before the Michigan situation) begun taking a look at it again. The all-digital clocks apparently can now be reprogrammed to display tenths of a second without added expense.

A separate issue relates to tying the whistle to the clock, like the NBA does. That technology, we're told, would be more difficult to deploy in a football stadium.

Making that whistle-clock connection even more challenging would be the "officiating mechanics" that allow a sequence that seemed to consume six seconds to be revised without extemporaneous explanation to take only one second.

Regardless, precision is important. Especially in the ongoing Wild West age of gambling. In a clock-based game, the clock should be respected with complete accuracy.

For now, between the clunky delay-of-game protocol (which gives the offense a little extra time to start the play but who knows how much?) and the idea that certain plays officially take less time than they actually did, pro football's commitment to time seems to be less like basketball and more like soccer — where the game ends whenever the referee decides it has ended.

item.title: Bo Nix: I saw Jalen Ramsey, just didn't throw it high enough over his head on interception
item.dc:creator: Michael David Smith
item.description: Broncos quarterback Bo Nix threw a truly baffling pick-six to Steelers cornerback Jalen Ramsey in Friday's loss, and afterward he said it was just a bad throw, not a bad read.
item.content:encoded:
Broncos quarterback Bo Nix threw a truly baffling pick-six to Steelers cornerback Jalen Ramsey in Friday's loss, and afterward he said it was just a bad throw, not a bad read.

Nix threw the ball directly to Ramsey, who was not particularly close to any Broncos receiver, which led to questions about what Nix was looking at. Nix said he thought he could throw the ball deep over Ramsey's head and threw it way too short.

"I saw him, just didn't throw it high enough over his head," Nix said.

The Steelers' first touchdown was also Nix's fault, as he dropped the football into the end zone, where T.J. Watt jumped on it.

"Going down 7-0 with a fumble recovered in the end zone for a touchdown is not ideal," Nix said. "That started us off on the wrong foot and we couldn't get out of the hole after that."

It was a miserable game from Nix, but he said the Broncos will move on to the next game. One in which they hope their quarterback won't hand the other team two touchdowns.

item.title: Mason Rudolph: Aftermath of Aaron Rodgers on Pat McAfee was challenging for Steelers
item.dc:creator: Michael David Smith
item.description: "We obviously had a lot of stuff we had to filter through, and a lot of aftermath with his visit on national television," Rudolph said.
item.content:encoded:
Steelers quarterback Mason Rudolph said after beating the Broncos on Black Friday that the situation with Aaron Rodgers gave the team an additional challenge preparing for the game.

Asked about Rodgers, Rudolph answered carefully but made clear that he didn't appreciate Rodgers going the Pat McAfee Show with a scorched-earth attack on coach Mike McCarthy.

"Very hard, very challenging," Rudolph said. "On one hand, you're thankful for the time you spent with him and everything you learned football-wise, and the friendship, but we obviously had a lot of stuff we had to filter through, and a lot of aftermath with his visit on national television. Unfortunate, but we turn the page."

Rudolph said his teammates told him they were confident in him as their starting quarterback, which he appreciated.

“They all had the same mixed emotions that I did," Rudolph said. "Like just shocked, what on earth just happened? When you wake up Wednesday morning. I thought that after the initial shock sort of passed through, they just made it known they were with me, behind me, and it wasn’t like a throw in the towel, season’s over vibe. . . . They had my back and I appreciate that."

Rudolph also said his teammates are behind McCarthy, who did a great job leading the team in the aftermath of releasing Rodgers.

“It was impressive," Rudolph said. "Neither of us had every been through that kind of week, plus you add in the short week. So I just can’t say enough. He’s obviously handling a multitude of managerial things and statements and press conferences, and then also taking the time to make sure that his playcalling responsibilities are first and foremost. I mean, unbelievable week. He balanced a lot. Proud of the way our team rallied around him and made it known, like, Dude we’re behind you. Let’s block out the noise and go win a game.”

The Steelers played perhaps their most impressive game of the season in Rudolph's first start, and made a strong statement that they can win without Rodgers.

item.title: Rams guard Bill Murray out for season after torn Achilles in first career start
item.dc:creator: Michael David Smith
item.description: A former undrafted rookie defensive lineman, Murray worked for years to reach the point where he could start on the offensive line.
item.content:encoded:
Rams guard Bill Murray got the first start of his NFL career on Wednesday against the Packers. It will also be his last game of the season.

Murray suffered a torn Achilles tendon in the game and will miss the rest of the season, according to Jeremy Fowler of ESPN.

The 29-year-old Murray had a long and difficult road to reach the point where he was starting in the NFL. He originally signed with the Patriots as an undrafted free agent defensive tackle out of William & Mary and spent three seasons on the practice squad. The Patriots liked his athletic profile and work ethic, and when he couldn't crack the gameday lineup on defense, they moved him to the offensive line, but after three years and only one game played, they released him.

Murray then signed with the Bears, got on the field as a backup offensive lineman for three games in two years in Chicago, and was released again.

In 2025, Murray returned to the Patriots' practice squad, got cut, then signed with the Colts' practice squad, and got cut again.

At the start of training camp this year Murray signed with the Rams, and after the Rams lost offensive linemen Coleman Shelton and Dylan McMahon to injuries last week, Murray finally got his chance to start this week.

That lasted three quarters, and now Murray's season is over.

item.title: Mike McCarthy admits he hasn't spent enough time with the defense
item.dc:creator: Mike Florio
item.description: McCarthy vows to take a closer look at the situation in the offseason.
item.content:encoded:
After registering an unlikely 27-5 win over the previously 8-2 Broncos, Steelers coach Mike McCarthy wasn't angry, resentful, or defiant.

He was the same guy he always is, and he admitted that (as former Steelers quarterback Aaron Rodgers said this week), McCarthy hasn't been sufficiently invested in the side of the ball that isn't his personal expertise.

"I have not spent enough time with the defense," McCarthy told reporters. "You know, and that’s something that, as far as job responsibility, job description, you know, these are things that'll be looked at in the offseason. But, you know, it’s a point in our year where we’re making adjustments and definitely conscientious of it. But at the end of the day, we have to all do our jobs and make sure we're giving the players the plan and all the other things that they need that we can perform and play with that type of urgency, physicality that we played today.”

McCarthy prefaced his comments with a lesson he learned as a boy, growing up in Pittsburgh.

"My father used to tell me all the time as a kid, 'You tell the truth, you only have to tell your story once,'" McCarthy said.

The truth is that this week has entailed two sharply different versions of reality, where both things can indeed be the truth. One, McCarthy (like all of us) has flaws. Two, Rodgers should not have spoken about them publicly.

Rodgers clumsily defended his decision to break the code of a football locker room by texting this to Al Michaels: “The code or sanctity exists to protect the integrity of the locker room, not to provide immunity from accountability for its leadership."

That's fine, but how does disregarding the "sanctity" of the locker room (a word Rodgers undoubtedly selected in response to Tom Brady using it on Thursday) create "accountability"? McCarthy is accountable to team owner Art Rooney II. Not to the media or the fans.

Also, who decides when breaking the code is justified in the name of "accountability" to people to whom McCarthy isn't directly accountable? There's no tribunal to whom Rodgers can apply for permission to disregard the privacy of a football team's inner workings. He took it on himself.

And to what end? He was either doing it to help the Steelers save their season, or he was lashing out.

We'll let you decide which explanation is more likely.

item.title: Kyle Shanahan: Brock Purdy's ankle sprain is "more mid than low"
item.dc:creator: Mike Florio
item.description: 49ers quarterback Brock Purdy emerged from Sunday's win over the Vikings with an ankle injury.
item.content:encoded:
49ers quarterback Brock Purdy emerged from Sunday's win over the Vikings with an ankle injury. He'll miss Sunday's game against the Seahawks. Whether he'll miss any games beyond that remains to be seen.

“It's too soon, but I'm pretty optimistic about it," coach Kyle Shanahan told reporters on Friday. "But, I was about this week to start and then it changes, so hopefully it'll be all right.”

Next Sunday, the 49ers visit the Giants. The following weekend, the Rams visit.

Shanahan also revealed some details about the specific nature of the ankle sprain.

“Anytime it's not a high ankle sprain, you get pretty relieved, but it was more mid than low, which is a little bit worse," Shanahan said. "Kind of had a feeling just the way it was by the time Wednesday came around. Didn't heal up as fast as we wanted, so had to shut him down.”

Shanahan added that surgery isn't on the table for Purdy.

Purdy's performance in 2026 has made him one of the favorites to win the NFL MVP award.

item.title: Mike Macdonald on Sam Darnold, when healthy: "I think he's done a good job"
item.dc:creator: Mike Florio
item.description: Quarterback Sam Darnold is back as Seattle's starter this week, after missing two games due to quad and rib injuries.
item.content:encoded:
Quarterback Sam Darnold is back as Seattle's starter this week, after missing two games due to quad and rib injuries. It's an opportunity to improve on what has been a challenging start to the 2026 season.

On Friday, coach Mike Macdonald was asked to assess Darnold's performance when healthy.

"I think he’s done a good job," Macdonald said. "As a football team, we’ve been good enough to go 6-4, and we want to get better. Yeah, he’s right there with everybody else.”

Well, he's not right there with the player who replaced him. Drew Lock has started three games and played all but one drive of another. His record is 4-0. Darnold is 2-4.

And their numbers are starkly different. Darnold has thrown 10 touchdown passes and nine interceptions. Lock has thrown seven touchdown passes and no interceptions.

Lock's passer rating is 125.6. Darnold's is 79.5.

Lock's games have come against the Patriots, the Cardinals twice, and the Raiders. Darnold has faced the Commanders, Chargers, 49ers, Broncos, Chiefs, and Bears — a much tougher slate of opponents.

The Seahawks won a Super Bowl with Darnold. That counts for something. Still, they're 6-4. They have an opportunity to get a seventh win on Sunday, with Brock Purdy out for the game against the 49ers.

item.title: NFL Playoff Picture 2026: Updated AFC and NFC standings, bracket, tiebreakers for Week 12
item.dc:creator: Michael David Smith
item.description: The Steelers' dominant win over the Broncos showed they remain in the thick of the playoff race after the Aaron Rodgers fiasco.
item.content:encoded:
The Steelers' dominant win over the Broncos showed they remain in the thick of the playoff race after the Aaron Rodgers fiasco. Here's the state of the playoff picture heading into Sunday of Week 12:

AFC Playoff Picture

DIVISION LEADERS

1. Bills (10-1): Inside track for the No. 1 seed after beating the Chiefs on Thanksgiving night.

2. Broncos (8-3): Currently ahead of the Chiefs in the AFC West based on the better record in common games

3. Jaguars (7-3): Loss to the Giants was a big blow to their hopes of earning the No. 1 seed in the AFC.

4. Bengals (7-3): In control of the AFC North, but Monday night's loss in Washington hurts.

WILD CARDS

5. Chiefs (8-3): Big loss to the Bills on Thanksgiving night.

6. Steelers (7-4): Their Black Friday win over the Broncos answers any questions about the direction of this team after cutting Aaron Rodgers.

7. Browns (6-4): Cleveland's path to the playoffs is looking surprisingly easy.

OUTSIDE LOOKING IN

8. Patriots (5-5): Hard to see them competing without Drake Maye.

9. Texans (4-6): Running out of time to go on a run.

10 Raiders (4-7): The rest of the season is about developing Fernando Mendoza.

11. Ravens (4-7): Lamar Jackson's injury just about killed their playoff hopes.

12. Jets (3-8): Aaron Glenn is on the hot seat.

13. Colts (3-8): No longer competing.

14. Chargers (1-9): The NFL's most disappointing team.

15. Dolphins (1-9): The playoffs this year were never a realistic possibility.

16. Titans (1-9): Need to figure out if Cam Ward is their quarterback.

NFC Playoff Picture

DIVISION LEADERS

1. 49ers (9-1): Inside track for the No. 1 seed after a big win Sunday night against the Vikings.

2. Bears (9-2): Thanksgiving win gave them first place in the NFC North.

3. Giants (6-3-1): Clear path to the playoffs in John Harbaugh's first season.

4. Panthers (5-5): Best record in the NFL's worst division.

WILD CARDS

5. Lions (8-3): Big loss to the Bears drops them down into wild card position.

6. Vikings (7-3): Have lost three of their last four after a hot start.

7. Rams (7-4): Big win on Thanksgiving Eve against the Packers moved them back into playoff position.

OUTSIDE LOOKING IN

8. Seahawks (6-4): Sunday's game in San Francisco is a big one.

9. Packers (6-5): The Thanksgiving Eve loss to the Rams dropped them out of playoff position.

10. Commanders (4-5-1): Still have a chance to catch the Giants in the NFC East.

11. Cowboys (5-7): The Thanksgiving meltdown was devastating to their playoff hopes.

12. Eagles (4-7): It's too little, too late for their playoff hopes, but the Eagles have played well in back-to-back wins over the Steelers and Cowboys.

12. Buccaneers (3-7): Still in the race in the terrible NFC South.

13. Falcons (3-7): Still in the race in the terrible NFC South.

14. Saints (3-7): Still in the race in the terrible NFC South.

16. Cardinals (3-8): Worst team in the NFC.

item.title: No Aaron Rodgers? No problem. Steelers crush Broncos with dominant defense
item.dc:creator: Michael David Smith
item.description: Mason Rudolph did enough on a day when the Steelers' defense made life miserable for Bo Nix.
item.content:encoded:
Aaron Rodgers was the story of the week in the NFL, but the story of today's game in Pittsburgh was the Steelers' defense.

Broncos quarterback Bo Nix could do nothing in Pittsburgh, as the Steelers' defense dominated in a 27-5 win.

Steelers quarterback Mason Rudolph, starting for the first time since Aaron Rodgers was benched and released, played reasonably well, completing 9 of 15 passes for 142 yards, with one touchdown and no interceptions. The Steelers didn't ask Rudolph to do a lot, but what they asked him to do, he did.

But the Steelers' defense was outstanding. T.J. Watt recovered a Nix fumble in the end zone for one touchdown, Jalen Ramsey returned a Nix interception for another touchdown, and the Steelers' defense had a great day on a rainy Black Friday in Pittsburgh.

The win improves the Steelers' record to 7-4 and erases any doubt that head coach Mike McCarthy can lead them to the playoffs this season. The loss drops the Broncos to 8-3, and raises questions about how far they can go with Nix at quarterback.

item.title: Justin Herbert ruled out, DJ Uiagalelei to make first start vs. Patriots
item.dc:creator: Myles Simmons
item.description: It is officially going to be DJ Uiagalelei vs.
item.content:encoded:
It is officially going to be DJ Uiagalelei vs. Tommy DeVito on Sunday.

Chargers quarterback Justin Herbert has been ruled out with a concussion suffered during last week’s loss to the Jets.

He did not practice all week.

Uiagalelei made his debut earlier this month against Houston, completing 2-of-7 passes for 24 yards with a touchdown.

Herbert has completed 62.4 percent of his passes for 1,851 yards with eight touchdowns and 11 interceptions so far this season.

Linebacker Daiyan Henley (knee) and running back Keaton Mitchell (knee) are also out.

Outside linebacker Akheem Mesidor (ankle) and receiver Brenen Thompson (hamstring) are doubtful.

item.title: 49ers announce Mac Jones will start vs. Seahawks, Brock Purdy is out
item.dc:creator: Michael David Smith
item.description: Purdy's ankle injury will force him to miss his first game of the season.
item.content:encoded:
Mac Jones will start at quarterback for the 49ers on Sunday against the Seahawks.

Brock Purdy, who is an MVP candidate this season, has not practiced all week with an ankle injury, and on Friday, head coach Kyle Shanahan confirmed that Purdy has been ruled out. Shanahan said Jones is ready to go and will play well on Sunday.

"Mac's been awesome," Shanahan said. "He's had a great week. We went through this with him last year so everyone's got a ton of confidence in Mac. Mac's had a hell of a camp and he's the same guy every day. It's been a good week with Mac."

Last year Jones started eight games while Purdy was hurt, and although Jones didn't play as well as Purdy, he did play well enough for the 49ers to go 5-3 in those eight games.

Now the 49ers will hope Jones can play well enough to beat the defending Super Bowl champions in a game that has major implications for the NFC playoff race.

item.title: Aaron Rodgers: Sanctity of the locker room doesn't protect the coach from accountability
item.dc:creator: Michael David Smith
item.description: With Al Michaels calling today's game in Pittsburgh, ex-Steelers quarterback Aaron Rodgers texted Michaels to give his side of the nasty breakup he just had with the team and head coach Mike McCarthy.
item.content:encoded:
With Al Michaels calling today's game in Pittsburgh, ex-Steelers quarterback Aaron Rodgers texted Michaels to give his side of the nasty breakup he just had with the team and head coach Mike McCarthy.

During the fourth quarter of the Broncos-Steelers game, Michaels read a text from Rodgers, in which Rodgers claimed he in no way violated the sanctity of the Steelers' locker room when he went on Pat McAfee's show to detail his problems with McCarthy.

"A lot of talk about the sanctity of the locker room," Rodgers said in the text Michaels read during the game. "The code or sanctity exists to protect the integrity of the locker room, not to provide immunity from accountability for its leadership. They took this public. Never heard from the head coach. Then they leaked at 11 p.m. They also barred me from the facility. That's why I went to McAfee."

Rodgers told McAfee that McCarthy, among other issues, wasn't watching enough film, was sleeping in team meetings, and addressed the team as the "Packers" instead of the Steelers during halftime on Sunday.

McCarthy's Steelers are dominating the Broncos today, which stands as a rebuke to Rodgers' claim that McCarthy isn't fit to be the team's coach. But Rodgers was able to get his side of the story into the game, via his text to Michaels.

Darnold has been listed as a full participant throughout the week after missing Seattle's last two games with a quad injury. Darnold had also suffered a cracked rib in the Week 8 loss to the Bears.

Darnold has had turnover issues this season, throwing nine interceptions this season. He’s thrown at least one pick in each of his last six starts.

Seattle is 3-4 in games that Darnold has started and 3-0 in games with Lock as QB1. Lock also brought the Seahawks back in the Week 1 win over the Patriots after Darnold exited due to injury.

Additionally, the Seahawks have ruled out right tackle Abe Lucas (ankle), left guard Quenton Nelson (knee), and defensive tackle Jarran Reed (toe) for Sunday’s game against the 49ers.

item.content:encoded:
Receiver Brandon Aiyuk is back, and he'll be back in the only number he's ever worn in the NFL.

Via multiple reports, Aiyuk and Commanders receiver Luke McCaffrey have struck a deal to give No. 11 to Aiyuk, who joined the practice squad two days ago.

McCaffrey will now wear No. 15.

The move strongly suggests that Aiyuk will be making his debut for the Commanders, sooner rather than later. And, at a more subtle level, that he's not being viewed by the organization as a guy who's getting a last chance to show that he still has gas in the tank, but as a player that the Commanders regard as someone who will step in and contribute.

Aiyuk won't play on Sunday at Arizona. He could be on the field as soon as Week 13, against the Titans.

item.dc:creator: Myles Simmons

item.content:encoded:
The Browns have signed a key special teams contributor to a new deal.

Cleveland announced on Friday that the club has signed long snapper Rex Sunahara to a four-year contract extension.

Sunahara grew up in Northeast Ohio in Bay Village, which is around 18 miles from where the Browns play at Huntington Bank Field.

"It's a dream come true. There's no place I'd rather be," Sunahara said, via Kelsey Russo of the team’s website. "There's no team I'd rather be with, so it's the best thing ever. It makes you really think about a lot of things, where the sacrifices that were made to help get me here, it makes you feel really good.”

Sunahara has appeared in 39 games for the Browns over the last three seasons, including all 17 last season and all 10 so far in 2026.

He and the rest of the Browns will play the Raiders on Sunday night this weekend.

item.title: Bo Nix throws directly to Jalen Ramsey for pick-six as Steelers dominate the first half
item.dc:creator: Michael David Smith
item.description: The Broncos' offense has been awful today.
item.content:encoded:
Broncos quarterback Bo Nix has been awful today in Pittsburgh. And he just made his worst play yet.

Nix threw a perfect pass directly to a wide-open Jalen Ramsey for a touchdown, which would be great if Ramsey played for the Broncos, but was not so great because Ramsey plays for the Steelers.

It's impossible to tell what Nix thought he was doing on the play, but he threw the ball right into Ramsey's hands, and Ramsey returned the interception 36 yards to the house for a pick-six that gave the Steelers a 24-5 lead.

It was the second Steelers defensive touchdown off a Nix turnover; Nix also dropped the ball in the first quarter and T.J. Watt recovered for a touchdown.

Steelers quarterback Mason Rudolph hasn't been great, but he's been a lot better than Nix, and the Steelers are rolling over the Broncos in the first half.

item.title: Alex Singleton tackles Jaylen Warren in the end zone for a safety as Steelers lead 14-5
item.dc:creator: Michael David Smith
item.description: The Broncos' offense can't do anything, but the defense has done something.
item.content:encoded:
On Black Friday in Pittsburgh, the defenses are outplaying the offenses.

The latest big play on defense came via Broncos linebacker Alex Singleton, who tackled Steelers running back Jaylen Warren in the end zone for a safety. That made the score 14-2 Steelers. On the subsequent possession, the Broncos kicked a field goal to make it 14-5.

More bad news for the Steelers came when linebacker Jack Sawyer was ruled out for the rest of the game with a knee injury.

Pittsburgh has two touchdowns, one of which came from the defense when T.J. Watt recovered a Bo Nix fumble in the end zone. The Steelers' other touchdown, a Mason Rudolph to DK Metcalf touchdown pass, was the game's only offensive score.

Rudolph has been better than Nix so far, which few would have expected heading into the game. But this game has been less about the quarterbacks than about the defenses.

item.title: Dan Quinn had an "absolutely fantastic experience" coaching with Mike McCarthy
item.dc:creator: Mike Florio
item.description: With Wednesday's rant from former Steelers quarterback Aaron Rodgers painting a negative picture about Steelers coach Mike McCarthy that extended to his time with both the Packers and the Cowboys, those who have worked with him in those places will inevitably be asked about McCarthy.
item.content:encoded:
With Wednesday's rant from former Steelers quarterback Aaron Rodgers painting a negative picture about Steelers coach Mike McCarthy that extended to his time with both the Packers and the Cowboys, those who have worked with him in those places will inevitably be asked about McCarthy.

Commanders coach Dan Quinn, who spent three years as McCarthy's defensive coordinator in Dallas, got the question on Friday.

"I had a like absolutely fantastic experience coaching with Mike," Quinn said, via Ben Standig. "He's part of the reason I wanted to go there. And over my three years with him, man, I learned a lot. So I can't speak anything from Pittsburgh but what I can say is like, you know, like I had an unbelievable coaching experience with him. Like, detailed about it. Got me better, challenged me in a lot of ways with how I'm thinking, what it can be, so that would go into it."

Some will say that Quinn is simply saying all the right things, and that he wouldn't want to make McCarthy look bad by telling tales of irregularities that may have transpired behind closed doors.

You know, like Rodgers should have done.

item.title: Mason Rudolph hits DK Metcalf for touchdown pass as Steelers take 14-0 lead over Broncos
item.dc:creator: Michael David Smith
item.description: It's been all Steelers in the first quarter in Pittsburgh.
item.content:encoded:
More than anyone else, the two players the Steelers needed to step up today were Mason Rudolph and DK Metcalf. And they did just that in the first quarter against the Broncos.

Rudolph threw a well-placed pass toward Metcalf, who leapt into the air over Broncos cornerback Patrick Surtain, reeled it in and landed in the end zone for a 22-yard touchdown.

It's the first start of the season for Rudolph, who has replaced Aaron Rodgers as the Steelers' quarterback. And it's the first game for Metcalf since his ejection last week against the Eagles drew him a great deal of criticism — not just for his two personal foul penalties, but for the poor play he has exhibited all season.

There's still plenty of time left, but in the first quarter, the Steelers look like they're firing on all cylinders. They're beating the Broncos 14-0.

item.title: Joe Milton III praises the Eagles, possibly criticizes the Cowboys
item.dc:creator: Mike Florio
item.description: Eagles quarterback Joe Milton III returned to Texas on Thursday and threw a significant wrench into the Cowboys' postseason plans (and, possibly, Philly's thinly-veiled soft tank).
item.content:encoded:
Eagles quarterback Joe Milton III returned to Texas on Thursday and threw a significant wrench into the Cowboys' postseason plans (and, possibly, Philly's thinly-veiled soft tank).

After the game, Milton reflected on his days in Dallas.

"It was a lot going through my head from when I first got here in Dallas to when I left, all the time I spent doing scout team quarterback, all the times where I was trying to get in the game, when they were up in games, just trying to get more experience," Milton said, via Nick Harris of the Fort Worth Star-Telegram. "I mean, it was just great coming back here and playing in this stadium in Jerry's World and seeing the guys that I worked hard with in fall camp and OTAs."

He then focused on his current team. While possibly adding a little commentary regarding his former team.

"But I mean, it's about the Eagles," Milton said. "These guys show up every day. Nobody's late to anything. Nobody's complaining about anything. That's all you can ask for. That's the most important thing that I love about this team. I just know they're going to keep fighting."

The obvious implication is that, in Dallas, some guys were not showing up every day. Some guys were late. Some guys were complaining.

There are surely complaints today, one day after the Cowboys lost their fourth game of the season while scoring 30 or more points.

item.title: Steelers score first as T.J. Watt recovers Bo Nix fumble in end zone
item.dc:creator: Michael David Smith
item.description: There hasn't been any offense on display in Pittsburgh so far on Black Friday, but there has been a touchdown.
item.content:encoded:
There hasn't been any offense on display in Pittsburgh so far on Black Friday, but there has been a touchdown.

On third-and-15 at his own 19-yard line, Broncos quarterback Bo Nix dropped back to pass and was immediately pressured, and he did about the worst thing he could have done: He dropped the football, which rolled into the end zone, where Pittsburgh's T.J. Watt fell on it for a touchdown.

It's 7-0 Steelers in the first quarter.

The player everyone is watching today is Steelers quarterback Mason Rudolph, making his first start of the season after Pittsburgh benched and then cut Aaron Rodgers. Rudolph hasn't done anything of note — he has just five passing yards through two Pittsburgh drives — but he hasn't made any big mistakes either.

Nix made a very big mistake, Watt capitalized, and that's the difference in the game so far.

item.title: Brandon Aiyuk will not play Sunday vs. Cardinals
item.dc:creator: Myles Simmons
item.description: While receiver Brandon Aiyuk joined the Commanders earlier this week, but his debut with the team will have to wait.
item.content:encoded:
While receiver Brandon Aiyuk joined the Commanders earlier this week, but his debut with the team will have to wait.

Head coach Dan Quinn confirmed to reporters in his Friday press conference that Aiyuk will not be elevated for Sunday's game against the Cardinals.

Aiyuk has only had a couple of practices with Washington, but he's impressed Quinn with his work so far.

“I think it’s not surprising, but I think the catch radius and how strong his hands were,” Quinn said. “I knew that, but I hadn’t seen it for couple of years I suppose. But, his aggressive nature to go get the ball and pluck it. He can get in and out of breaks very quickly. So, those were two of the things that caught my eye yesterday and today.

“But it’s a good first impression for sure. He’s like everybody else, working hard and trying to learn it. New faces, new scheme, new people. He’s off to a good start."

Aiyuk has not played since the 2024 season. His first opportunity to get on the playing field may come in Week 13 when the Commanders face the Titans on the road.
